name: Kamakura shogunate
info: The first feudal military government of Japan, founded by Minamoto no Yoritomo at Kamakura and later run by the Hōjō regents, remembered for repelling the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281.

facts.capital: Kamakura (the Imperial Court remained at Heian-kyō, Kyoto)
facts.predecessor: Heian system of Imperial rule; the Minamoto clan after the Genpei War

t: Minamoto no Yoritomo founded the shogunate after the Genpei War and governed from Kamakura, leaving the emperor and court in Kyoto as figureheads.
From 1203 the Hōjō clan held real power as shikken, regents of the shōgun, while Fujiwara and imperial princes served as figurehead shōguns.
The shogunate held off the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281, but their cost and the lack of rewards for its warriors weakened it before its fall in 1333.
dyk: When Nitta Yoshisada took Kamakura in 1333, about 870 members of the Hōjō clan, including the last three regents, committed suicide at their family temple, Tōshō-ji.
ev: Yoritomo establishes the shugo and the jitō, the year now most often taken as the shogunate's start
Minamoto no Yoritomo is appointed Seii Taishōgun
Minamoto no Sanetomo is assassinated, ending the line of Minamoto shōguns
Emperor Go-Toba's attempt to regain power fails in the Jōkyū War
The shogunate issues the legal code Goseibai Shikimoku
The first Mongol invasion under Kublai Khan is broken off after a destructive typhoon
The second Mongol invasion fails after some seven weeks of fighting in Kyushu and another typhoon
Nitta Yoshisada takes Kamakura and the shogunate is overthrown in the Kenmu Restoration

sections.foundation:
In earlier Japanese history civilian power lay with the emperor and his regents, drawn from the Imperial Court and the aristocratic clans, and military affairs were handled under the civil government. From 1180 to 1185 the Taira and Minamoto clans fought the Genpei War. Minamoto no Yoritomo defeated the Taira and in victory seized power from the civil aristocracy, reducing the emperor and his court to symbolic figureheads.

Historians disagree about the year the shogunate began. The older and once most popular view took 1192, when Yoritomo was appointed Seii Taishōgun; the later prevailing view took 1185, when he established the shugo, who controlled military and police power in the regions, and the jitō, in charge of tax collection and land administration. Japanese history textbooks of 2016 give no single year. Yoritomo governed autocratically from the eastern city of Kamakura, while the emperor and court stayed in the official capital, Heian-kyō.
sections.socioeconomy:
The shogunate rested on the land. Its stewards, the jitō, were placed in the manors (shōen) and received revenues from them in return for military service. They worked alongside the gesu, who delivered the manor's dues to its proprietor in Kyoto, so that the dual system of military and civil government reached down to the manor itself.

Warriors expected land as a reward for service. The defensive war against the Mongols left no gains to distribute to those who had fought, which led to discontent. For two decades after 1281 the shogunate kept watch against another invasion, and the strain on the military, the financial expenditure and the cost of building defensive walls weakened the regime considerably. The Hōjō monopoly of power, together with these unrewarded sacrifices, fed resentment among its vassals.
sections.military:
The shogunate's greatest test came from the Mongols under Kublai Khan. Fifty years earlier it had agreed to Korean demands to deal with the wokou raiders, and the resulting good relations meant the Koreans, under Mongol occupation, passed intelligence to Japan. The shogunate rejected Kublai's demands for submission. In 1274 a combined force of about 40,000 Mongols and Korean conscripts landed with some success, but the defenders were not routed, and a typhoon destroyed one-third of the invading force.

When Kublai again demanded submission, the Hōjō had the messengers executed and prepared: a wall was built round the hinterland of Hakata Bay, defensive posts and garrison lists were set up and ships were built to harass the invaders. In 1281 some 50,000 Mongol, Korean and Chinese troops and about 100,000 conscripts from the defeated Song fought for some seven weeks in Kyushu without strategic gain. Another typhoon destroyed at least one-third of the Mongol force, and troops left ashore were slaughtered by the samurai. The storm was credited as the "divine wind", kamikaze.
sections.governance:
The shogunate worked within the framework of the Heian system of Imperial rule. Yoritomo made a chancellery, the mandokoro, his principal organ of government; under the Hōjō a separate council, the hyōjōshū, became its focus. Military governors (shugo) were appointed over the provinces, mostly from powerful local families, alongside the civil governors (kokushi) sent from Kyoto. In 1232 the government issued the legal code Goseibai Shikimoku, used into the Muromachi period, and set up a court of appeals, the Moncho-jo.

After Yoritomo's death in 1199, Hōjō Tokimasa claimed the regency (shikken), which became hereditary in the Hōjō clan, and his daughter Hōjō Masako became so powerful that she was called the "nun shogun". The Minamoto line ended when Sanetomo was assassinated in 1219. Later shōguns came from the Fujiwara and then from imperial princes, while the Hōjō regents ruled. The regime lasted 135 years under 9 shōguns and 16 regents.
sections.impact:
The Kamakura shogunate began the long age of military government in Japan. By taking power from the civil aristocracy, Yoritomo made the emperor and court figureheads, a pattern the later shogunates kept. Its offices, the shugo over the provinces and the jitō in the manors, carried military rule into every province and down to the manor, and its legal code, the Goseibai Shikimoku, remained in use into the following period.

Its system was a pyramid of nominal and real authority: the Hōjō regents had taken power from the Minamoto, who had taken it from the emperor, yet regents, shōguns and emperors all kept their titles side by side. Its defence against the Mongols, in which the invasions were ended by heavy losses and the exhaustion of the Korean state that supplied them, gave rise to the idea of the kamikaze, the "divine wind" that saved Japan from foreign invasion.
sections.decline:
The power of the Hōjō went unchallenged after the Jōkyū War until 1324, when Emperor Go-Daigo plotted to overthrow them; the plot was discovered almost at once. In 1331 Go-Daigo took up arms against Kamakura but was defeated by the shogunate's commander Ashikaga Takauji and exiled to Oki Island. When a warlord came to the exiled emperor's aid, the Hōjō sent Takauji to attack Kyoto, but once there he changed sides and supported Go-Daigo.

At the same time Nitta Yoshisada, another warlord loyal to the emperor, attacked and took Kamakura in 1333. About 870 members of the Hōjō clan, among them the last three regents, committed suicide at their family temple, Tōshō-ji, whose ruins have been found in today's Ōmachi. Imperial rule was restored in the Kenmu Restoration until 1336, when Ashikaga Takauji made himself shōgun and founded the Ashikaga shogunate.

summary: The Kamakura shogunate, founded by Minamoto no Yoritomo after the Genpei War, ruled Japan from Kamakura between 1185 and 1333. Its real masters from 1203 were the Hōjō regents. It built a system of shugo and jitō, issued the Goseibai Shikimoku and repelled two Mongol invasions, but their cost weakened it until Go-Daigo's supporters destroyed it.
references: Mass, Jeffrey P., The Kamakura bakufu: a study in documents (Stanford University Press, 1976)
Mass, Jeffrey P., Warrior government in early medieval Japan: a study of the Kamakura Bakufu, shugo and jitō (Yale University Press, 1974)
Nussbaum, Louis-Frédéric and Käthe Roth, Japan encyclopedia (Harvard University Press, 2005)

pointDescs.1185: Yoritomo establishes the shugo and the jitō after victory in the Genpei War.
pointDescs.1192: Yoritomo is appointed Seii Taishōgun and the military government in Kamakura is formally set up.
pointDescs.1199: Yoritomo dies in an accident, leaving the Minamoto weakened.
pointDescs.1204: Loyalists of Yoriie rise against the Hōjō, who defeat them and assassinate Yoriie.
pointDescs.1219: Sanetomo is assassinated by his nephew Kugyō, ending the Minamoto shōguns; the Hōjō are in total control.
pointDescs.1221: Go-Toba's attempt to regain power fails in the Jōkyū War.
pointDescs.1232: The Goseibai Shikimoku legal code is issued.
pointDescs.1274: The first Mongol invasion is broken off after a typhoon.
pointDescs.1281: The second Mongol invasion fails in Kyushu.
pointDescs.1301: Two decades of watch against the Mongols strain the regime's army and finances.
pointDescs.1324: Go-Daigo's first plot against the Hōjō is discovered and foiled.
pointDescs.1331: Go-Daigo takes up arms, is defeated and exiled to Oki Island.
pointDescs.1333: Nitta Yoshisada takes Kamakura and the Hōjō commit suicide at Tōshō-ji.

notes: Start year disputed in the article (1185 or 1192); register's 1185 used and both stated.
Point 1301 is a turning point inferred from 'two further decades' of watch after 1281; the year itself is not in the article (Hōjō Sadatoki's regency ends 1301 in its list).
